newsitem.title: FRANCE: France probes theft of Elf-Gabon papers.
newsitem.headline: France probes theft of Elf-Gabon papers.

text.p: France on Tuesday opened a preliminary investigation into the disappearance from police offices of documents linking an Elf Aquitaine oil company Swiss bank account with Gabon President Omar Bongo, a justice ministry spokesman said.

"(Justice) Minister Jacques Toubon wants all light to be shed on this incident and will impose the strongest punishment if the investigation shows these are warranted," the minister's spokesman told reporters.

The documents, which were under seal and disappeared last weekend, had been used to assist Paris judge Eva Joly's ultra-sensitive investigation into the oil firm's activities in the west African state, police sources said.
Bongo telephoned French President Jacques Chirac earlier this month to voice anger at Joly's investigation amid reports the probe was causing a crisis between Paris and its oil-rich former colony.

The chairman of Elf's Gabon subsidiary, Andre Tarallo, is under judicial investigation in France for receiving the proceeds of misuse of corporate funds but he is free on 10 million francs ($1.8 million) bail.
Judicial sources have said Tarallo told Joly he had opened a bank account in Switzerland that was used solely by Bongo.
The newspaper Le Monde said earlier this month that Elf chairman Philippe Jaffre was then flying to Libreville to try to calm Bongo's anger over the freezing of the Swiss account at Joly's request.
Le Monde said the veteran Gabonese leader had threatened Chirac with "economic sanctions" and had also sent an angry letter to Jaffre, who heads the main foreign oil firm operating in Gabon.
Joly is in charge of investigations over alleged fraud at Elf while former French railways chief Loic Le Floch-Prigent was chairman in 1988-93, involving the payment of alleged covert commissions.
Joly placed Le Floch-Prigent in preventive detention last year but he was released in December after six months.
Le Monde wrote on Tuesday that the documents disappeared from the offices of a police's anti-corruption division recently shaken by politically-motivated internal rivalry.
Extreme rightist leader Jean-Marie Le Pen said the case "proved government intelligence agents worked hand-in-hand with crooked politicians."
